The short-tailed chinchilla (Chinchilla chinchilla) is a medium-sized hystricognath rodent native to the high Andean plateaus of Peru, Bolivia, Chile, and Argentina. Neonates emerge from the reproductive tract after an extended gestation period that, under the standard thermoneutral body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], lasts approximately 128 days [tg = approximately 128 days]. This duration places the species among the longest gestation periods documented for its body size, reflecting the advanced state of development at parturition. Newborn pups typically weigh around 35 grams [Wwb = around 35 grams], a value consistent with observations in the closely related long-tailed chinchilla and indicative of the substantial maternal investment that precedes delivery. The altricial neonates are fully furred and have their eyes open, yet they remain entirely dependent on maternal milk. Parturition generally occurs during the austral spring, when the availability of high-quality forage in the puna ecosystem reaches its seasonal peak, supporting the energetic demands of early lactation. Females typically give birth to litters ranging from 1 to 6 pups [N_R_i = litters ranging from 1 to 6 pups], with an average litter size of two offspring that is well within the typical range for chinchillid rodents. The female can produce up to two litters annually [F_R_i = up to two litters annually], a reproductive frequency that, when combined with the moderate litter size, yields a moderate annual reproductive output and may be limited by the extended gestation interval required for single pups to develop fully before delivery.

Weaning in the short-tailed chinchilla takes place approximately 49 days after birth [tx = approximately 49 days after birth] when the mother maintains a core body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This milestone marks the nutritional independence of the offspring, which transition from a solely milk-based diet to consuming the fibrous grasses, forbs, and shrubs characteristic of their high-altitude habitat. The pups begin sampling solid food around three weeks of age, but full cessation of nursing does not occur until the seventh week, providing a gradual dietary transition that ensures adequate nutrient intake during a critical growth phase. Weaning weight typically reaches 150 to 200 grams, reflecting the substantial mass gain achieved during the suckling period. The timing of this transition is ecologically significant because the annual window of peak plant productivity in the puna is relatively short, spanning only a few months; thus, offspring that gain independence earlier in the growing season have more time to build fat reserves before the onset of the harsh dry winter. Sexually mature individuals then follow a different growth and developmental trajectory, with females capable of conceiving their first litter relatively soon after reaching adulthood.

Puberty, defined here as the age at which individuals first become capable of breeding, is reached at approximately 240 days after birth [tp = approximately 240 days after birth] under an ambient body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This relatively rapid attainment of sexual maturity for a rodent of this body size is notable and contrasts with the slower maturation schedules observed in certain other hystricognaths. Females experience their first estrus shortly after reaching this developmental milestone, and males show fully descended testes and active spermatogenesis by the same age. The timing of puberty in wild populations is likely influenced by nutritional condition and the quality of the forage available during the juvenile growth period, with individuals born early in the breeding season reaching maturity in time to breed during the following year's reproductive window. Subadult males, although reproductively capable, may not gain immediate access to breeding females due to the hierarchical social structure of wild colonies, where dominant males monopolize mating opportunities. Consequently, the effective age at first reproduction for males may be delayed relative to the physiological onset of puberty, reflecting the interplay between life history and social dynamics in this species.

Adult short-tailed chinchillas attain a characteristic ultimate body mass of approximately 600 grams [Wwi = approximately 600 grams], with the reported range extending from 400 to 800 grams across individuals and populations. This size places the short-tailed species at the larger end of the size spectrum among chinchillids, consistent with its adaptation to the cooler, more thermally demanding environment of the high Andes. Body mass varies seasonally, with adults accumulating fat reserves during the austral summer months and losing condition during the dry season when food resources become scarce. Basal metabolic rate, measured in captive individuals under thermoneutral conditions at a body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], averages 226.3 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 226.3 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This metabolic rate is low relative to what would be predicted for a rodent of this mass using standard allometric equations, suggesting that the species exhibits metabolic adaptations to its oxygen-poor high-altitude environment. The reduced metabolic rate likely contributes to energy conservation in an ecosystem with sparse, low-quality forage and may also reflect the animal's sedentary habits, as wild chinchillas are not highly active foragers but instead feed on nearby vegetation from their rocky refuges.

Maximum lifespan in the short-tailed chinchilla, documented from both captive records and field observations, reaches approximately 20 years [am = approximately 20 years] when maintained at a typical body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], a remarkably long duration for a rodent of its body size. One of the longest-lived individuals was recorded at 22 years and 4 months in a zoo collection, but the species-level maximum is consistently reported as two decades across multiple sources. This extreme longevity is a classic example of the slow life history syndrome observed in many caviomorph rodents, which combine extended gestation, small litter sizes, delayed reproductive maturity relative to other rodent clades, and prolonged postnatal development. The combination of a 128-day gestation period and a 20-year lifespan places the species at the extreme slow end of the mammalian life history continuum. This extended lifespan also means that adults can accumulate considerable reproductive experience over many breeding seasons, potentially enhancing the survival prospects of their offspring through improved maternal care. Given the species' endangered status in the wild due to historic overhunting for the fur trade and ongoing habitat degradation, understanding the demographic implications of its slow life history is essential for effective conservation planning, as populations may recover only slowly from disturbance.
